## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. The *sampling distribution* of a statistic describes:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The values in a single sample</li>
  <li>The values in the population</li>
  <li>How the statistic varies across many possible samples of the same size</li>
  <li>How the population parameter varies across many possible populations</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Sampling distributions are distributions of *statistics*, not of data. One dot on a sampling distribution corresponds to one summary statistic (e.g., $\bar{x}$) computed from one sample.</div>
:::

Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. What does it mean to construct a 95% confidence interval?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>There is a 95% probability that the population parameter lies in the interval</li>
  <li>95% of the data values fall in the interval</li>
  <li>If we repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter</li>
  <li>The sample mean has a 95% chance of being correct</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> The 95% refers to the long-run reliability of the *procedure*, not the probability for any single computed interval. The parameter is fixed; the interval is random.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Estimation with the bootstrap

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. In bootstrapping, you generate replicate samples by:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Drawing without replacement from the population</li>
  <li>Drawing with replacement from the original sample</li>
  <li>Drawing without replacement from a different population</li>
  <li>Generating random numbers from a normal distribution</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Bootstrap = resample *with replacement* from your one observed sample. This simulates &quot;what would another sample have looked like?&quot; without needing the actual population.</div>
:::

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. A wider confidence interval generally means:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>More precision</li>
  <li>Less precision (more uncertainty)</li>
  <li>A larger sample</li>
  <li>A higher confidence level always</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Wider = more uncertain about where the parameter is. To narrow a CI, lower the confidence level (e.g., 90% instead of 99%) or collect more data.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Case study: is yawning contagious?

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. As a rough rule, **doubling** your sample size (with everything else unchanged) typically:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Doubles the CI width</li>
  <li>**Narrows the CI by about a factor of $\sqrt{2}$** — standard error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$</li>
  <li>Has no effect on CI width</li>
  <li>Automatically raises the confidence level</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Standard error scales like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so doubling $n$ shrinks the SE — and roughly the CI half-width — by a factor of $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4$. To **halve** the CI width you'd need *four times* the data. This is the practical reason &quot;collect more data&quot; is the answer to &quot;I need a tighter estimate&quot; — it works, but with diminishing returns.</div>
:::

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q5. To **narrow** a 95% confidence interval **without changing the data**, you can:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Increase the confidence level</li>
  <li>**Decrease the confidence level** (e.g., to 90%)</li>
  <li>Take fewer samples</li>
  <li>You can't narrow it</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Lowering confidence narrows the CI — but you trade away long-run reliability. Be honest about this trade-off when you choose a confidence level.</div>
:::
